title: Similarity Search
explain: Similarity search finds the `k` nearest vectors to a query vector. Brute force compares against every vector and is exact but too slow at scale, so production systems use approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes that trade a little recall for big speedups: IVF cells, HNSW graphs, compressed codes. (近似换速度, 用 recall 衡量损失.)
model:
**Exact:** compare the query with all `n` vectors, `n x d` multiply-adds. 10M x 768 = 7.68 billion per query: fine under about a million vectors or on a GPU, hopeless beyond.

**ANN families**

| Index | Idea | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **IVF** | cluster vectors with [k-means](#/sd/f/k-means) into `nlist` cells; scan only the `nprobe` cells closest to the query | more probes: more recall, more work |
| **HNSW** | layered proximity graph, greedy walk from coarse to fine layer | fast and accurate, memory hungry, slow to build |
| **PQ** | compress vectors into short codes | less memory, some recall loss; often with IVF |

```
IVF query:  embed ─▶ compare to nlist centroids ─▶ pick nprobe cells
            ─▶ scan those vectors ─▶ top-k ─▶ (re-rank)
```

**Recall@k** = fraction of the true top-k the index returns. Tune `nprobe` or HNSW `ef` until recall meets the target at acceptable latency.

Vectors come from [item embeddings](#/sd/f/item-embedding), compared with [similarity](#/sd/f/similarity), candidates re-ranked with [top-k ranking](#/sd/f/top-k-ranking).

details.q: When is brute force the right answer?
details.a: Up to roughly a million vectors, or when batched on a GPU, or when you need exact results (evaluation ground truth). It has no index to build or maintain, and recall is 100%. Always keep it as the oracle for measuring an ANN index's recall.

details.q: How many distance computations does an IVF query take?
details.a: Centroid comparisons plus the scanned cells. With 1,000,000 vectors in `nlist` = 1,000 equal cells and `nprobe` = 10: 1,000 + 10 x 1,000 = 11,000, about 1.1% of a brute-force scan. Raising `nprobe` raises cost roughly linearly.

details.q: How do you measure the quality of an ANN index?
details.a: Recall@k against exact search on a sample of queries. If the true top 5 is {a,b,c,d,e} and the index returns {a,c,x,e,y}, recall@5 is 3/5 = 0.6. Plot recall against latency while sweeping `nprobe` or `ef` and pick the knee for your SLO.

details.q: A true neighbour is missed with `nprobe` = 1. What do you do?
details.a: It likely sits just across a cell boundary from the query. Probe more cells (raise `nprobe`) and accept the extra latency; or use more, smaller cells, or switch to HNSW. A single cell is exact search again.

details.q: A marketplace takes the top 10 neighbours and then drops out-of-stock items. Only 2% are in stock. What goes wrong?
details.a: Post-filtering an unfiltered top 10 leaves about 0.2 items on average, often none. Filter during the search (filter-aware graph traversal), pre-partition by the filter (tenant, region), or over-fetch far more candidates and filter after.

details.q: What happens as vectors are updated and deleted?
details.a: Indexes degrade: IVF cells go stale as the data drifts away from the trained centroids, HNSW leaves tombstones, and both fragment. Plan periodic rebuilds, write into a small fresh index and merge, and track recall over time.

ANN retrieval is a cheap, coarse candidate stage. A second stage with a heavier model, exact distances or business rules orders the few hundred candidates, so you can tune recall and precision separately.

prompts.q: Explain exact versus approximate nearest-neighbour search and when you need each.
points: Brute force is n x d per query, exact
Fine up to about a million vectors or on a GPU
ANN trades a little recall for large speedups
Keep exact search as the evaluation oracle

prompts.q: Walk through an IVF query and its tuning knobs.
points: k-means cells at build time, nlist
Compare query to centroids, scan nprobe cells
Cost = nlist + nprobe x cell size
More nprobe: more recall, more latency

prompts.q: Design semantic product search with an 'in stock' filter and updates.
points: Embed items offline, query online with the same model
Post-filtering a small top-k returns almost nothing
Rebuild or merge indexes as data changes
